# In Praise of Moss

There is a kind of attention that the world rarely rewards, and moss is its patron saint.

Most of us walk past moss the way we walk past the grout between tiles. It is background, the green fuzz on a north-facing wall, the soft patch at the base of a tree, the thing a landscaper scrapes off a roof. And yet moss is one of the great success stories of life on Earth. Its ancestors were among the first plants to crawl out of the water and onto bare rock, somewhere around 470 million years ago, long before there were trees, flowers, or anything that could be called soil in the modern sense. In a real way, moss and its early relatives helped *make* the ground the rest of the terrestrial world now stands on. They broke down stone and trapped dust, and they died and decayed into the first thin layers of organic earth.

What fascinates me most is how moss succeeds by declining nearly every strategy we associate with success in plants.

It has no true roots. Instead it has rhizoids, fine threads that anchor it but do little to draw up water. It has no internal plumbing to speak of, no vascular system to lift fluid skyward, so it cannot grow tall. It has no flowers and no seeds. Its sperm must literally swim through a film of water to reach an egg. By the logic of a sunflower or an oak, moss is a collection of disadvantages.

But moss has made a different bargain. Because it cannot pull water from deep underground, it absorbs moisture directly through its leaves, often just a single cell thick. And because it cannot guarantee a steady supply, it has learned to let go. Many mosses are what biologists call *poikilohydric*: they don't fight to maintain their internal water. When the air dries, they dry with it, curling up, going brittle and brown, shutting down their metabolism almost entirely. They look dead. They are not. Add water and within minutes to hours they unfurl, green up, and resume photosynthesis as if nothing happened.

This capacity can stretch across astonishing spans of time. In 2014, researchers reported that moss frozen beneath Antarctic ice for over 1,500 years began growing again when thawed in the lab. Fifteen centuries of suspended animation, and then, simply, life resuming.

I find something moving in that. We tend to imagine resilience as toughness: armor, resistance, holding the line. Moss suggests another model. Its resilience is surrender without defeat, the ability to become very small and very still, to wait out the bad season, and to trust that rain will come. It doesn't resist drought so much as decline to be destroyed by it.

---

Moss also rewards the kind of looking we rarely do. From standing height, a mossy log is a smear of green. Kneel down, and it becomes a forest. The botanist and writer Robin Wall Kimmerer, in her book *Gathering Moss*, describes this shift beautifully: how moss is best known not through binoculars but through a hand lens, how its world only opens once you get close enough to see individual leaves glinting like tiny spears or feathers or stars.

And that miniature forest is inhabited. Tardigrades, the famously indestructible "water bears," are frequently found living in moss, drying out and reviving alongside it. Rotifers, nematodes, and mites move through the stems like animals through a jungle. There's even evidence that some mosses are "pollinated," in a sense, by tiny arthropods called springtails, which carry sperm from plant to plant much as bees carry pollen. A 2012 study found that springtails were attracted to scents released by fertile female moss plants. Long before flowers and insects struck their famous deal, moss may have been running a quieter, older version of it.

---

Humans, when we have paid attention, have found moss remarkably useful. Sphagnum moss, the peat-forming kind, can hold many times its own dry weight in water, often cited as around twenty times. Its cells include large, empty, porous chambers that act like a sponge, and it creates an acidic, low-oxygen environment that discourages bacterial growth. During the First World War, when cotton was scarce, volunteers in Britain, Canada, and elsewhere gathered huge quantities of sphagnum to be made into wound dressings. It was absorbent, mildly antiseptic, and it grew for free in bogs.

Those same bogs are, quietly, among the most important landscapes on the planet. Peatlands cover only around three percent of Earth's land surface but store an enormous amount of carbon, by common estimates more than all the world's forests combined. Sphagnum builds them slowly, layer upon layer, the living moss growing on top while the dead moss beneath fails to fully decay in the waterlogged, acidic conditions. Over thousands of years, that undecayed material accumulates into peat. The same chemistry is why bogs have preserved human bodies for millennia, the so-called bog people of northern Europe, with skin and hair and even expressions intact.

So the humble green carpet turns out to be a carbon vault, a medical supply, an archive of the dead, and an ecosystem in miniature.

---

In Kyoto there is a temple, Saihō-ji, better known as Kokedera, the Moss Temple, whose garden is covered in over a hundred varieties of moss. Visitors must apply in advance, and before walking the grounds they are often asked to copy Buddhist sutras by hand. It's a lovely piece of design, whether or not it was intended as such: you arrive slowed down. By the time you see the moss, your attention has already been adjusted to its scale and tempo.

I think that's what moss asks of us more broadly. Not reverence exactly, but a recalibration. It is a reminder that not all flourishing is vertical, that not all strength looks like strength, and that some of the oldest and most consequential work on Earth is being done low to the ground, slowly, by things that do not ask to be noticed.

The next time rain falls after a dry spell, somewhere near you a patch of brown, brittle-looking moss will unfurl and turn green again. It's done this for hundreds of millions of years. It will probably be doing it long after us.
